contributions: REST, a stress-testing evaluation framework that transforms any existing single-question reasoning benchmark into a more challenging multi-question variant via cyclic-indexed question concatenation, requiring no new question creation or human annotation effort

a large-scale evaluation of 30+ LRMs (1.5B-671B, open and proprietary) across 9 reasoning benchmarks, revealing that even SOTA models exhibit substantial performance degradation under multi-question stress, challenging the assumption that strong single-question LRMs are general multi-problem solvers

evidence that REST sharply increases benchmark discriminative power, revealing large performance gaps among models with near-identical, near-ceiling single-question accuracy, and that downstream post-training on single-question tasks does not reliably transfer robustness to multi-question settings

a mechanistic diagnosis, via error-type categorization, question-position analysis, and quantitative attention-allocation measurement, identifying the 'overthinking trap' (attention drift toward a model's own prior reasoning traces rather than the current question) as a primary cause of REST performance degradation, and demonstrating that Long2Short-trained (concise-reasoning) models are substantially more robust to this stress
limitations: REST is primarily empirical and exploratory, serving as a controlled proxy for increasing reasoning load that may not fully match real-world multi-context task structures. It slightly increases evaluation cost, since multi-problem prompts generally require longer reasoning sequences and thus more computational overhead, though the paper's appendix analysis found the latency increase not significant and acceptable. The current evaluation focuses exclusively on textual reasoning tasks; since REST's core concatenation mechanism is inherently modality-agnostic, it could naturally extend to multimodal reasoning scenarios (e.g. simultaneously processing multiple charts or diagrams), but this extension is left to future work.
method: REST transforms an existing benchmark Q = {q_1,...,q_N} into stressed prompt sets by concatenating s consecutive questions (with cyclic indexing so every question appears exactly s times across all prompts and exactly once in each of the s possible positions, guaranteeing fair question coverage) into a single instruction, instructing the model to answer each sub-question with its own boxed/code-block answer; the stress level s is varied per benchmark by difficulty (s in {1,3,6,9,12} for simple benchmarks like GSM8K/ARC-C/BBH; {1,3,5,7,9} for medium ones like MATH500/AMC23; {1,2,3,4,5} for hard ones like AIME24/25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench). Evaluates 30+ LRMs (1.5B to 671B parameters, including proprietary o3-mini/o4-mini/Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking) across 9 reasoning benchmarks, reporting Single (original) and Stress (REST, averaged across stress levels >1) accuracy. To diagnose the cause of degradation, manually categorizes failures into six types (Output Truncation, Endless Repetition, Format Violation, Question Omission, Summary Error, Reasoning Error) across four representative models on AIME24; measures per-question-position reasoning-token allocation and accuracy via a position heatmap; and quantifies attention drift by computing, for the tokens generating the answer to the last question Q_N, the fraction of attention mass (averaged over layers/heads/generated tokens) allocated to relevant content (Q_N and its own reasoning) versus distractor content (earlier questions Q_<N and their reasoning traces A_<N).
one_liner: REST (Reasoning Evaluation through Simultaneous Testing) concatenates multiple questions from an existing benchmark into a single prompt to stress-test LRMs' multi-context reasoning; across 30+ models and 9 benchmarks it finds even SOTA models like DeepSeek-R1 degrade substantially (e.g. -31.6% on AIME25), that the 'overthinking trap' is a primary cause, that Long2Short-trained models are more robust, and that REST reveals sharp performance gaps among models that look identical under traditional single-question evaluation.
problem: Standard LRM evaluation presents one question at a time, which (1) is vulnerable to data contamination and diminishing discriminative power as models approach near-ceiling accuracy on widely-used benchmarks, forcing a costly, human-effort-intensive cycle of continuously creating new, harder benchmarks, and (2) fails to evaluate models under multi-context pressure -- reasoning across multiple simultaneous queries -- a requirement of real-world deployment scenarios (batched conversation turns, multi-bug code review, multi-criteria compliance audits) that existing multi-question-prompting studies have only tested on simple tasks (text classification, commonsense QA), not reasoning-intensive ones.

relevance.overthinking: Directly central to the topic and explicitly names the 'overthinking trap' as a primary driver of a large-scale, systematically measured failure mode: it provides quantitative, attention-level evidence (not just accuracy curves) that overthinking -- generating unnecessarily long, redundant reasoning traces -- causally hurts models specifically because that redundant reasoning becomes attentional noise a later part of the same generation must compete against, which is a distinct mechanistic angle from most of this archive's other overthinking accounts (which focus on wasted tokens within a single question, not interference across multiple questions in one context). Its finding that Long2Short-trained (efficient-reasoning) models are more robust under this specific stress test is an unusually direct, large-scale (30+ model) empirical validation that overthinking mitigation has real downstream benefits beyond the single-question benchmarks it is normally evaluated on.

results: LRMs handle several simple questions robustly (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B's GSM8K accuracy drops only 0.43% under REST) but this robustness collapses on harder benchmarks: even DeepSeek-R1 suffers a 29.1% accuracy drop on AIME24 and 31.6% on AIME25 under REST, and smaller models degrade more sharply (R1-7B's AIME24 accuracy falls from 54.17% single to 16.53% under stress). REST substantially amplifies discriminative power among models that look near-identical under single-question evaluation: on MATH500, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (93.0% single) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (94.6% single) differ by only 1.6 points, but under REST the 7B model plummets to 66.75% while the 32B model retains 88.97%, a 22.22-point gap invisible in standard evaluation; the same pattern holds for models fine-tuned on the same base (AReaL-boba-RL-7B and Light-R1-7B-DS both start from R1-7B and score slightly higher than it single-question, but both degrade to a similar or worse level under REST -- 60.77% and 61.73% versus R1-7B's 66.75% -- showing downstream post-training on single-question tasks does not transfer robustness to multi-question settings, and can even exacerbate degradation at higher stress levels). Error analysis (six-category taxonomy, AIME24) shows performance drops are NOT primarily due to models exceeding the maximum output token length (Output Truncation is a minor cause for most models tested); for strong models like DeepSeek-R1, Question Omission (overlooking later questions, a 'question position bias') and Reasoning Error together account for 42.00% of failures, while for weaker models like Light-R1-7B, Endless Repetition and Output Truncation dominate (48.90% combined) -- reflecting that smaller models' limited capacity is more exposed by REST's stress. No Format Violation errors occur for any of the four analyzed models, confirming degradation stems from genuine reasoning limitations rather than prompt-format artifacts. Question-position analysis (heatmaps across model sizes/benchmarks) confirms questions appearing earlier in a stressed prompt consistently achieve higher accuracy than later ones, and models allocate a disproportionately large share of their token budget to earlier questions, leaving insufficient reasoning capacity for later ones ('adaptive reasoning effort allocation' -- present in high-performing models like GPT-OSS-120B, which allocates tokens evenly and uses fewer tokens per question on average -- is identified as a critical factor for strong REST performance, in contrast to low-performing models like R1-7B). Topic-grouped versus random question concatenation makes negligible difference (<0.6 points across four models on MATH500), ruling out topical relatedness/interference as the driver of degradation. Attention-drift analysis quantitatively confirms the 'overthinking trap': post-trained models with sharper REST degradation devote more attention, when answering the final question, to their own prior (irrelevant) reasoning traces rather than to the current question -- e.g. AReaL-boba-RL-7B (65.0% relative accuracy drop) allocates 27.2% attention to distractor prior reasoning versus only 52.2% to the relevant current-question content, while Qwen3-8B (40.6% relative drop, notably less degradation) allocates only 2.1% attention to prior reasoning while maintaining 63.2% on relevant content -- directly linking the overthinking phenomenon (unnecessarily long, redundant reasoning) to REST's observed performance collapse via a measurable attentional mechanism. Models trained with the 'Long2Short' technique (introducing a length-reward term to promote concise, efficient reasoning) show markedly better REST robustness: L1-Qwen-1.5B-Max surpasses the untrained R1-1.5B by a 44.71-point accuracy margin at stress level s=9 on MATH500, and error analysis confirms Long2Short training mitigates not only length-related failures but also broader reasoning-degradation patterns under multi-question stress.
